source: Unicode Technical Standard #35, Unicode Locale Data Markup Language (LDML), Part 1: Core; https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr35/
quote: The subdivision codes designate a subdivision of a country or region. They are called various names, such as a state in the United States, or a province in Canada. The codes in CLDR are based on ISO 3166-2 subdivision codes.
reading: Reading: an established standard code exists for an area below the country, built on the country code (ISO 3166-2, as CLDR carries it). That gives (b) and (c) a key to use beside the country; it does not choose between (b), areas for some rules, and (c), areas for any rule.

source: Unicode Technical Standard #35, Unicode Locale Data Markup Language (LDML), Part 1: Core; https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr35/
quote: ISO 3166-2 subdivision codes may change over time, because each country may change the codes it supplies to ISO. Typically this does not cause problems for use in locale identifiers. Newly added ISO 3166-2 codes are added to CLDR in each release. If an ISO 3166-2 code is removed, it remains valid in CLDR, though marked as deprecated. If an ISO 3166-2 code is replaced by a new code, an alias is added to CLDR that maps the old code to the new code.
reading: Reading: on what happens when the area changes, the standard shows that the area's code itself changes: codes are added, deprecated (kept valid) and aliased old-to-new. A rule keyed on an area, under (b) or (c), then needs codes kept valid after removal and a mapping from old code to new. It bears on the cost of (b) and (c) alike, not on which to take.

source: Unicode Technical Standard #35, Unicode Locale Data Markup Language (LDML), Part 1: Core; https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr35/
quote: In some unusual cases, countries have been known to reuse codes, giving a code a very different meaning from what it had.
reading: Reading: a subdivision code can be reused for a different area, so a key stored as the bare published code can change its meaning under past records. This bears on how an area is held under (b) or (c), as a stable identifier of one's own mapped to the published code, and on (c)'s dated area; it weakens neither option.

source: Unicode Technical Standard #35, Unicode Locale Data Markup Language (LDML), Part 1: Core; https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr35/
quote: For example, “en-GB-u-rg-uszzzz” represents a locale for British English but with region-specific defaults set to US for items such as default currency, default calendar and week data, default time cycle, and default measurement system and unit preferences.
reading: Reading: localisation data lets region-specific defaults, default currency among them, be read from a key whose syntax admits a subdivision (the valid values are unicode_subdivision_id), though the standard says a value other than the whole region would be unusual. It shows an established design that keys a currency default on a field able to name an area within a country, the form (c) describes, while noting such use is rare.
note: Line 1089 of the same file states the valid values: 'The valid values are a unicode_subdivision_id of type “unknown” or “regular”; [...] (Usage of anything other than zzzz would be unusual, though.)'

kind: provider's own documentation (Google API design types)
quote: // Optional. Highest administrative subdivision which is used for postal / // addresses of a country or region. / // For example, this can be a state, a province, an oblast, or a prefecture. / // For Spain, this is the province and not the autonomous / // community (for example, "Barcelona" and not "Catalonia"). / // Many countries don't use an administrative area in postal addresses. For / // example, in Switzerland, this should be left unpopulated.
reading: Reading: an address carries one area below the country, optional, at the level the postal system uses, which need not be the level a rule answers to (province, not the larger region). An area read from the business record's address, as (c) proposes, is then only as present, and at only the level, that the country's postal practice gives; a rule keyed on another level would need the area held apart from the postal field. It bears on how (c) reads the area, not on whether to take it.
note: ' / ' marks a line break in the captured file.

source: Stripe API reference, The Tax Registration object; https://docs.stripe.com/api/tax/registrations/object
reading: Reading: a payment provider's tax product keys a tax registration on a state within a country, beside the country, and dates it (the same object's fields active_from and expires_at). It supports (b), an area as a key for a tax rule, with dates on the registration. It shows nothing on payment services or currency keyed on an area.
note: ' / ' marks a line break. The object's fields: 'Time at which the registration becomes active.' (text.txt line 200) and 'If set, the registration stops being active at this time.' (line 221); the state field's own description sits under a collapsed 'Show child attributes' and is not in the visible text.

kind: established data project's documentation (OpenStreetMap, community-maintained wiki)
quote: Due to cultural and political differences, admin levels of different countries only correspond approximately to each other.
reading: Reading: in a hierarchy of places used across countries, the levels below the country do not line up between countries, so 'an area within the country' must be named per country (which level a rule keys on). It adds a per-country definition to (b) and (c) alike; it does not weaken either.
note: Line 57 of the same file: 'admin_level=2 through admin_level=10 allow for different administrative subdivision schemes to be handled in a consistent way by data consumers.'

source: Martin Fowler, Temporal Property (Further Enterprise Application Architecture draft, 2004); https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/TemporalProperty.html
quote: You will always see an accessor function that takes a Time Point as an argument: this allows you to ask “what was Mr Fowler's address on 2 Feb 1998?”.
reading: Reading: the established pattern for a property that changes over time, an address being the pattern's own example, holds it with dates and reads it as of a time point. It supports (c)'s dated area on the business record, and each order keeping the area that served it; it says nothing on which rules key on the area.

source: Martin Fowler, Temporal Property (Further Enterprise Application Architecture draft, 2004); https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/TemporalProperty.html
quote: Remember that it's not difficult to refactor a regular property into a temporal one.
reading: Reading: the pattern's author holds that making a property dated later is a small change to the code. That weakens the part of (c)'s case that rests on the cost of adding dates later, as far as the code goes; it does not speak to past records kept without dates, which the register names as what a retrofit cannot recover.

source: SIX, Data Standards (ISO 4217 Maintenance Agency page); https://www.six-group.com/en/products-services/financial-information/market-reference-data/data-standards.html
kind: standard's maintenance body page (ISO 4217 Maintenance Agency)
quote: SIX is the official Maintenance Agency of these currency codes under ISO 4217 and as such the only recognized, authoritative source on currency code designations.
reading: Reading: names the body whose lists say when a code is given; the source's kind, not a finding on the options.
note: Kept as the authority for the next row. The quote has a no-break space after SIX, as captured.

source: SIX, Data Standards (ISO 4217 Maintenance Agency page); https://www.six-group.com/en/products-services/financial-information/market-reference-data/data-standards.html
kind: standard's maintenance body page (ISO 4217 Maintenance Agency)
quote: Changes to the currency codes lists occur if a currency is created, withdrawn or parts thereof altered.
reading: Reading: the standard's lists change per currency: a code is added, withdrawn or amended when a currency is created, withdrawn or altered. What the page shows is one code per currency; it does not say what happens when one currency's units differ in value between areas, and the standard's own clause on that was not fetched (iso.org refused it, see notes-designs.md). On this page alone it bears on (a), a currency being its code, and neither supports nor weakens (c).
note: The page's FAQ, line 183: 'Whenever a new currency needs to be added to list one or a currency needs to be amended or deleted from the respective lists two or three.'

source: Martin Fowler, Money (Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture catalog, 2003); https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/money.html
quote: If all your calculations are done in a single currency, this isn't a huge problem, but once you involve multiple currencies you want to avoid adding your dollars to your yen without taking the currency differences into account.
reading: Reading: the pattern holds a currency with every amount, so amounts in different currencies are not combined unconverted. Under (c) two currency areas under one code would be two such currencies; whether the pattern's currency is a code or a record is not said on this page (the book's chapter 18 was not read). It supports a currency on every amount, which (a), (b) and (c) share; it does not choose among them.
note: The page's own heading: 'Represents a monetary value.'

source: Unicode Technical Standard #35, Unicode Locale Data Markup Language (LDML), Part 1: Core; https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr35/
quote: In protocols, the currency codes should always accompany any currency amounts; otherwise the data is ambiguous, and software is forced to use the user's territory to guess at the currency.
reading: Reading: localisation data identifies an amount's currency by its code, and holds the code's link to regions and periods apart (line 989 of the same file). That is (a)'s form, a currency being its code; nothing there names an area within a code with its own value. It supports (a) as the established form; it does not show (c) failing.
note: Line 989 of the same file: 'Supplemental Currency Data provides the list of countries (regions) and time periods associated with each currency code.'

quote: The class is designed so that there's never more than one Currency instance for any given currency. Therefore, there's no public constructor.
reading: Reading: a platform's money type identifies a currency by its ISO 4217 code ('Currencies are identified by their ISO 4217 currency codes', line 34), one instance per code. Two currency areas under one code can't be two instances of this type; a design under (c) would hold its own currency record beside it. It supports (a) as the common platform form and shows what (c) has to add.
note: Line 38 of the same file: users may supersede a country's currency data, with 'An optional UTC timestamp may be specified per currency entry if users need to specify a cutover date indicating when the new data comes into effect.'

source: Stripe API reference, The PaymentIntent object; https://docs.stripe.com/api/payment_intents/object
quote: Three-letter ISO currency code, in lowercase. Must be a supported currency.
reading: Reading: a payment provider's money record carries its currency as a bare ISO code beside the amount. A payment sent to such a provider can carry only the code, whatever Sharrwah holds inside; under (c) the area would stay on Sharrwah's own records. It supports (a) at the provider boundary, and bears on (c) only as a mapping from record to code at that boundary.

quote: Ledgers partition accounts into groups that may represent a currency or asset type or any other logical grouping. Only accounts on the same ledger can transact directly, but you can use atomically linked transfers to implement currency exchange.
reading: Reading: a ledger database holds the currency of each account and transfer as a number the application defines, not as a code, with the currency's details kept elsewhere (line 32: 'You may want to store additional metadata about each ledger in a control plane database.'). Amounts that refer to an application's own currency record is the form (c) and S02-M6 describe; it supports (c)'s form, in one ledger design.

quote: Accounts and transfers are immutable once created. In order to change the asset scale of a ledger, you would need to use a different ledger number and duplicate all the accounts on that ledger over to the new one.
reading: Reading: in this design a change to a currency's unit is a new currency record (a new ledger number), not an edit to past amounts. It bears on (c): a currency whose value differs is held as a separate record, the shape (c) gives a second area under one code; it does not show that one code with two such records is needed.
